electrodeposited Cu/Sn bimetallic catalyst Huaxin Li 1 , Xian Yue 1 , Yunsheng Qiu 2 , Zhou Xiao 1 , Xianbo Yu 1 , Chao Xue 1 , Junhui Xiang 1 *
1 Center of Materials Science and Optoelectronics Engineering, College of Materials Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, People’s Republic of China 2 Advanced Energy Materials Laboratory, College of Materials Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, People’s Republic of China
* Corresponding author. Prof. Xiang Junhui
E-mail address: xiangjh@ucas.ac.cn
Electrocatalysis is considered to be an effective method for carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction to formate (HCOOH) and achieving renewable energy conversion. Unfortunately, limited by the high overpotentials, low selectivity and poor stability of the existing catalysts, the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction is far from practical application. Herein, we designed a series of CuxSny (x,y are the molar ratio) bimetallic alloy catalysts by co-electrodeposition strategy for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction(CO2RR) to HCOOH generation. Bimetallic CuxSny catalysts are found to be more efficient than their monometal counterparts due to metal synergistic effects. In more details, the Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst delivers high selective for HCOOH evolution of above 85 % over a wide potential range (−0.8 V to −1.0 V vs. RHE) with a low onset potential of −0.6 V vs. RHE, exhibit a Faradaic efficiency of 91.38% towards HCOOH generation and a maximum current density of 13.79 mA cm −2 at −0.8V vs. RHE. Furthermore, after long-term (36 hours) operation, the Faraday efficiency of the catalyst is still higher than 88.35%. This work paves a facile way to synthesize novel bimetallic electrocatalysts for efficient production of HCOOH.
Key words: CO2RR; Bimetallic catalysts; Co-electrodeposition; Formate

With the rapid development of global industry and the increase of energy demand, the
consumption of fossil fuels such as oil and natural gas increases steadily, and the emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere is considerable, which leads to global warming and climate change [1,2]. In order to solve above problems, a variety of strategies have been reported and the following two methods are representative: (1) reducing CO2 emissions [3,4]; (2) designing a reasonable experimental scheme to convert CO2 into valuable C products such as methanol [5], methane [6], formate [7,8], ethanol [9], ethylene [10,11], etc. Compared with the traditional catalytic reduction of CO2 at high temperature and high pressure, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (CO2RR) in a mild reaction conditions with high conversion efficiency presents great application potential [12,13]. In addition, electricity can be converted from clean energy such as wind energy, tidal energy and solar energy, so as to efficiently realize the recycling of resources. Therefore, CO2RR is considered as an effective way to achieve CO2 conversion.
Formate (HCOOH) is considered to be the most potential candidate in various products of
CO2RR [14]. It is a non-toxic and harmless chemical raw material, which is of great significance in industrial production (such as medicine, rubber, organic synthesis and other fields), and can be directly used as fuel [15,16,17]. Therefore, formate presents high commercial value. Many studies have shown that metals such as Pd [18], Pb [19], Cu [20] , Hg [21], and Sn [22,23] can effectively reduce CO2 to HCOOH in the electrocatalytic process. Although the noble metal Pd shows excellent catalytic activity and selectivity, it is difficult to achieve large-scale production due to its high price and unavailable. And Pb and Hg are rarely used in CO2RR because of their toxicity. As an environmentally friendly and economical metal, Sn-based monatomic materials, oxides, alloys and carbon supported Sn are ideal catalysts. Some research notes that both Sn and SnOx contribute to the selectivity and activity of CO2 reduction [24,25]. Liu et al [26], reported a Sn/SnO2 nanoparticle catalysts and found that the Sn/SnO2 composites exhibited high FEHCOO − of >70% at a wide potential range from −0.8 to −1.4V vs. RHE. However, these catalysts still exhibit high overpotential and low current density. Besides, Cu-based catalysts have been found to be outstanding in the production of various hydrocarbons, aldehydes and alcohols in previous studies [27,28,29,30]. It has shown that Cu has high reactivity, low overpotential and high selectivity for formate. Yang et al [31], prepared Cu nanoparticles embedded in carbon substrate (Cu NPs@C) as electrocatalysts and found that Cu nanoparticles are responsible for the high faradaic efficiency of HCOOH of 78% at −1.0 V vs.RHE and yield of 82.8 μmol h −1 cm −2 at −1.2 V vs.RHE. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the properties of metals are often changed due
to the introduction of other metals to form alloys, especially under the synergistic effect of bimetallic, the CO2 adsorption intensity, catalytic activity and selectivity will change [33,34]. In the past few years, great progress has been made in the fabrication of Cu-based and Sn-based alloy materials by numerous synthesis strategies, such as CuPd [35,36], CuZn [37], CuSn [38], and PdAu [39] bimetallic alloy materials. Nevertheless, the traditional alloy synthesis strategy is difficult to control the morphology of the catalyst, thereby limiting the electrochemical active area and reducing the catalytic reaction active sites, which will affect the catalytic activity of the catalyst. Distinctively, electrochemical deposition is one of the effective methods to prepare alloy materials, which can control the amount of electron and proton exchange in electrolyte by controlling the circuit. As an effective synthesis method, electrodeposition technology usually applies metal base (such as copper mesh, copper foil, copper foam, etc.) or carbon base (such as carbon cloth, carbon fiber, etc.), and two steps or mutil-steps to synthesize alloys [40]. Similarly, co-electrodeposition is an effective method to prepare alloy materials as well. Huan et al [41], prepared Au–Ag bimetallic nano dendrite constructed through a simple one-step co-electrodeposition on a Pt surface. Choi et al [42], fabricated Ag-Cu dendrite catalysts by an electrodeposition method for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. With above merits, co-electrodeposition is undoubtedly a simple and effective method to prepare Cu/Sn alloy electrocatalysts.
Herein, a facile co-electrodeposition synthesis strategy was adopted to prepare Cu/Sn
bimetallic alloy electrocatalysts. The optimized catalytic performance of the catalysts can be adjusted by controlling the molar ratio of Cu/Sn in the catalyst. In this research, we designed a series of CuxSny (x,y are the molar ratio) bimetallic alloy catalysts by co-electrodeposition strategy for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to HCOOH generation(Fig.1). In particular, the large number of grooves in Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst provides a large surface area for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to HCOOH. Base on the properties of Cu/Sn bimetallic alloy, the study indicates a synergistic effect between Cu and Sn, which greatly promotes the electron and proton transport in the catalytic reaction process. Delightfully, the Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst exhibits excellent Faraday efficiency of HCOOH up to 91.38% at −0.8V vs.RHE and maintaining the

sections.heading: 2.2 Precursor solution preparation and catalyst co-electrodeposition
sections.text:
The co-electrodeposition method used in this work was reported by previous study [43].
CuxSny-CC catalysts were electrodeposited from CuCl2•2H2O and SnCl2•2H2O precursor solution (the total metals content of mixed precursor was always 0.02M). Na3C6H5O7•2H2O and Urea were added to the precursor solution to form metal complexes. The catalysts were named Cu-CC, Cu3Sn1-CC, Cu1Sn1-CC, Cu1Sn3-CC and Sn-CC by changing the metals content ratio of Cu 2+ /Sn 2+ in precursor solution. Before co-electrodeposition, carbon cloth (CC) was cleaned with HCl, ethanol and ultrapure water under ultrasonic wave to remove surface stains. For CuxSny-CC catalysts, cathodic co-electrodeposition was applied with a three-electrode cell using platinum wire as counter electrode, saturated calomel electrode as reference electrode and CC was used as working electrode. CuxSny was deposited onto carbon cloth by chronoamperometry at the potential of -0.75V for 10 hours to ensure the uniform deposition of Cu and Sn on carbon cloth.

sections.text:
The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction test was performed by CHI-760E electrochemical
workstation (Shanghai Chenhua Instruments Company). The working electrode (Cu xSny-CC catalysts) and reference electrode (Ag/AgCl) were placed in the cathode chamber, and the counter electrode (platinum sheet) was placed in the anode chamber. Before the

As shown in Fig. 2(c-g), Cu-CC is coated with a layer of fine Cu particles, while Sn-CC are irregularly large particles scattered on the carbon cloth, and Sn particles are not well coated on the carbon fiber. The TEM images of Cu-CC (Fig. S2(a)) and Sn-CC (Fig. S3(a)) show well-dispersed Cu and Sn particles, respectively. Cu3Sn1-CC, Cu1Sn1-CC and Cu1Sn3-CC bimetallic catalysts are more

Particularly, the as-prepared Cu1Sn3-CC (Fig. 2(g)) is connected by micro blocks and forms numerous grooves in the middle, which presents a layered petal structure. The difference of surface morphology of CuxSny-CC may be attributed to the influence of the ratio of Cu 2+ and Sn 2+ in the precursor on the deposition rate of Cu and Sn, and the synergistic effect of them around the carbon fibers. According to the data in Table S1, the hierarchical structure would effectively increase the electrochemically active area of the catalysts to increase the
electrochemically active centers. In addition, according to HRTEM test（Fig. 2(h)）, the crystal
plane spacing of Cu1Sn3-CC is about 0.2106 nm, which is confirmed to be the (110) crystal plane of Cu1Sn3-CC, indicating that Cu6.25Sn5 alloy was formed during the co-electrodeposition of Cu and Sn, which is consistent with the results of XRD (Fig. 3(a)).
The crystal phase of CuxSny-CC was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (Fig. 3a).
Compared with the standard mental Cu PDF card (JCPDS PDF #04−0836), the main diffraction peaks of Cu-CC (2θ= 43.29°, 50.43° and 74.13°) correspond to Cu (111), (200) and (220) crystal planes. In addition, the existence of Cu (111) crystal plane can be confirmed by HRTEM image of Fig. S3b. The diffraction peaks revealed for Sn-CC can be indexed as (200), (101), (220), (211) and (312) planes of mental Sn (JCPDS PDF #04−0673). Similarly, the HRTEM test of Fig. S4b further shows the existence of Sn (211) crystal plane, and the lattice stripe spacing is 0.2023nm. With the addition of Sn 2+ in the electroplating solution, the diffraction intensities of Cu (111) and Cu (200) decrease obviously. It is worth noting that when the molar ratio of Cu 2+ / Sn 2+
is 1:1 (Cu1Sn1-CC), a new crystalline phase of Cu41Sn11 (JCPDS PDF
#30-0510) appears, indicating the formation of Cu/Sn alloy and the existence of crystalline alloy phase. When the molar ratio of Cu 2+ / Sn 2+
is 1:3 (Cu1Sn3-CC), the diffraction peaks of
2θ= 30.13°, 42.97°, 53.36° and 62.63° correspond to (101), (110), (201) and (202) crystal planes of Cu6.25Sn5 (JCPDS PDF#47−1575), respectively. In addition, the weak diffraction peaks of Sn (101) and (102) planes appear in the XRD diffraction peaks of Cu1Sn1-CC and Cu1Sn3-CC, while Cu (111) decreases gradually and even disappears completely in Cu1Sn3-CC, indicating that the increase of Sn content is beneficial to the formation of Cu6.25Sn5 crystal.

Cu1Sn3-CC were characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to analyze their elemental compositions and chemical states (Fig3. (b)). XPS spectra show that as-prepared Cu1Sn3-CC is mainly composed of C, O, Cu and Sn, which is consistent with EDS results (Fig. S4). In addition, the surface elements of used Cu1Sn3-CC are C, O, Cu and Sn as well, which indicates that the chemical elements of Cu1Sn3-CC have not changed after long-term operation. The binding energy of Sn 3d5/2 and Sn 3d3/2 peaks locate at 489.49 eV and 492.89 eV, respectively, suggesting that the chemical state of Sn is between 0 and +4 in as-prepared Cu1Sn3-CC catalysts. The occurrence of 0-valence Sn could be due to the ratio of Cu 2+ / Sn 2+ in the precursor solution, which allows the excess Sn 2+ reduced to Sn (Sn 2+ →Sn), which is further confirmed by XRD results. However, after long-term operation, the chemical states of Sn 3d changed. According to the area ratio of peak position (Fig. S5), the chemical ratio of 0 chemical state and +2 chemical state decreases from 0.32:1 to 0.29:1, and the diffraction intensity of Sn in XRD test (Fig. S6) also decreases, indicating that Sn is easier to be oxidized in CO2RR durability test. The oxidation states of Cu 2p in the as-prepared Cu1Sn3-CC and used Cu1Sn3-CC exhibit similar states at 933.37 eV and 954.07 eV, corresponding to Cu/Cu + species. In order to identify the specific binding energy of Cu and Cu + , we measured the auger electron spectrum in Fig. 3 (f). sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical activities of CO2 reduction
sections.text:
The electrochemical performance of the catalyst was evaluated in CO2-saturated 0.5M
KHCO3 electrolyte. The current density and onset potential were measured by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), and the electrocatalytic activity was investigated. As shown in Fig. 4(a), pure Sn-CC exhibits poor activity, with onset potential of −0.65V vs. RHE and a total current density (normalized to geometric surface area) of 19.3 mA cm −2 at −1.0V vs. RHE. As a control, the onset potential of Cu-CC catalyst is −0.35V vs. RHE, which is much lower than Sn-CC. When CuxSny-CC is prepared by the co-electrodeposition, Cu and Sn are considered to be a mixed bimetallic alloy, which leads to a strong electronic interaction between Cu and Sn. Compared with the catalyst without Cu, this interaction shifts the initial potential of Sn to a positive direction. In particular, the onset potential of Cu1Sn3-CC is −0.6V vs. RHE, and the total current density of Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst is 34 mA cm −2 at −1.0V vs. RHE, which is much higher than other catalysts, showing excellent catalytic activity. Except current density and onset potential, selectivity is also an important index to evaluate catalytic performance. In general, HER reaction is an important competitive reaction of CO2RR. The LSV curves of Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst were obtained in CO2-saturated electrolyte and N2-saturated electrolyte at a scanning rate of 10mV s −1 , respectively (Fig. 4(b)). The onset potential (−0.79V vs. RHE) of Cu1Sn3-CC in N2-saturated electrolyte is much higher than that in CO2-saturated electrolyte (−0.6V vs. RHE), the difference is 190 mV, and the current density of Cu1Sn3-CC decreases to 9.8 mA cm −2
at −1.0V vs. RHE, which indicates that Cu1Sn3-CC can selectively
electrocatalytically reduce CO2 compared with HER reaction.

In addition, the stability of the Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst was investigated by electrolysis at
−0.8V vs.RHE for 36 hours. As shown in Fig. 5(a), there is no obvious fluctuation of current density during the whole electrolysis process, so is the SEM images (Fig. S9); and the total current density maintain at 16 mA cm −2 (normalized to geometric surface area). Compared with the previous few hours, the Faraday efficiency of HCOOH decrease slightly in the long-time electrolysis, but remain above 88.35%. Furthermore, we also tested NMR spectra of the electrolyte during the long-term durability test at −0.8V vs. RHE of Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst (Fig. 5(b)), the absorption intensity of HCOO - increase with the increase of catalytic time, indicating that Cu1Sn3-CC has excellent catalytic stability and selectivity.
The electrochemically active area (ECSA) can reflect the number of electrochemically
active centers of the catalysts. In order to evaluate the electrochemical activity of CnxSny-CC catalysts and control group, we measured the electrochemical active area of CnxSny-CC and calculated the electrochemical double-layer capacitance (Cdl) (ECSA was positively correlated with Cdl). As shown in Fig. S10, the Cdl of Sn-CC is only 0.23 mF, and the Cdl of Cu3Sn1-CC, Cu1Sn1-CC and Cu1Sn3-CC are 0.33 mF, 0.38 mF and 0.41 mF, respectively, indicating that the addition of Cu improves the Cdl of the catalysts. It is worth noting that ECSA of Cu1Sn3-CC is much higher than that of CnxSny-CC bimetallic catalysts (Table.S1), indicating that Cu1Sn3-CC has a larger electrochemical active area. From the SEM image of Cu1Sn3-CC (Fig. 2(g)), it can be seen a lot of groove-protrusion hierarchical structures, the hierarchical structures with large electrochemically active areas provide more adsorption active sites for improved CO2 gas adsorption and thus improved electrochemical performance.
The Tafel slope can be used to describe the kinetic characteristics of chemical reaction. As
shown in Fig. 5(c), the Tafel slope catalyzed by Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst is 128 mV dec −1 , which is smaller than other catalysts, indicating that Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst has a higher reaction rate when reducing CO2 to HCOOH. The Tafel value may come from the fact that the catalyst exposed more specific exponential crystal planes. According to the literature, the Tafel value of 118 mV dec −1 indicates that the process of obtaining the first electron is the rate control step of the whole reduction reaction [49]. However, the Tafel value in this work is obviously higher than 118 mV dec −1
, which indicates that the rate control step of CO2 reduction on Cu1Sn3-CC
surface is not a simple electron transfer process. It is widely believed that the initial binding strength and mode of the first intermediate on the catalyst surface have a great influence on the reaction pathway of CO2RR [50]. The reaction pathways of Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst

electrochemical reduction of CO2 to HCOOH and CO can be described by the schematic illustration in Fig. 6 and following equations [51]:
HCOOH: CO2 + e - + H + + * → *OCHO
*OCHO+ e - + H + → *HCOOH
*HCOOH → HCOOH(aq) + * CO: CO2 + e - + H + + * → *COOH
*COOH + e - + H + → *CO + H2O
*CO → CO(g) + *
Where * represents the surface adsorption site. In the reaction pathway of HCOOH product, CO2 molecules first form activated CO2* by adsorbing electrons, and then activated intermediate CO2* reacts with electron and proton transfer to form activated intermediate *OCHO. Furthermore, *OCHO adsorbs another electron and transfers proton to form intermediate *HCOOH, thus forming HCOOH product. However, intermediate *COOH and *CO were formed in the reaction path of CO product. This result further reveals that the CO2RR reaction is a multi proton/electron transfer electrochemical reaction.
The electrochemical impedance of the catalyst was measured in CO2-saturated 0.5M
KHCO3 solution. Fig. 5(d) shows the Nyquist curve of CnxSny-CC catalysts. By comparison, it is found that the slope of low frequency part of Cu-CC catalyst is the smallest and the material transfer resistance is the smallest, while the slope of low frequency part of Sn-CC catalyst is the highest, which is not conducive to the material transfer during the catalytic reaction. When Sn is doped with Cu, the slope of low frequency decreases, that is to say, the material transport resistance of the catalyst decreases. The radius of high frequency arc part Cu1Sn3-CC catalyst is the smallest, which is helpful for charge transfer. This result further confirmed the synergistic effect of Cu/Sn bimetallic in CO2RR. Low electron transfer resistance is conducive to the interaction between electrons and CO2 in the process of CO2 reduction, which accelerates the CO2 reduction rate; while low mass transfer resistance is contribute to the diffusion of CO2 and reduction products on the electrode surface, which improves the CO2 reduction activity.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we applied a facile way to prepared a series of CnxSny-CC bimetallic alloys
catalysts by co-electrodeposition, and explored their application in electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide to formate generation. Compared with single component metal catalysts and other conventional electrocatalysts, bimetallic alloy catalysts possess extraordinary electrocatalytic performance for CO2RR. The experimental results indicate that Cu1Sn3-CC
catalyst presents a wide potential range (−0.8V to −1.0V vs.RHE）and long-term (36 hours)
stability. And above 91.38% of HCOOH was generated with high selectivity at −0.8V vs.RHE. Tafel and electrochemical active area test further explained the catalytic mechanism and proved the synergistic catalytic effect of Cu/Sn bimetallic. This simple co-electrodeposition synthesis strategy provides guidance for the design of high efficiency and low-cost electrocatalysts, and also provide a facile technical way for the design of bimetallic alloy electrocatalysts.
